Corporate Restructuring

The Delaware Migration

"We aren't hiding the money. We're hiding the targets."

August 12, 2015 // 21:00 EST // "The Bridge", Stardust Studios
The Architecture of Silence

The heavy blast door to "The Bridge" was locked. Inside, the massive tracking board that monitored the O'Connell Family Trust's global assets was glowing quietly.

Holly O'Connell stood at the head of the conference table. Spread out before her were five identical stacks of heavy, legal-weight paper, each marked with a different colored tab. She looked exhausted, but her eyes held the sharp, dangerous clarity of a predator that had just finished digging a very deep trench.

Ryan rolled his wheelchair up to the table, eyeing the stacks. Evan and Tyler took seats on the flanks, while Cassidy stood by the window, looking out into the dark industrial park.

"I passed," Holly said simply.

Cassidy turned, a massive smile breaking across her face. "The Delaware Bar? Holly, that's four states! You're a machine."

Evan offered a low whistle. "Virginia, New York, California, and now Delaware. Are you trying to collect them like trading cards?"

"I'm trying to build a moat," Holly replied, tapping the thickest stack of paper. "Virginia has been good to us. It's our home. But legally? It's too loud."

Ryan frowned, locking the brakes on his chair. "Loud how? We don't do press. We haven't done an interview in eight years."

"Paperwork is loud, Ry," Holly explained, leaning against the table. "Back in 1997 during Hard Reset—right after the '$13.99 War' and Cassidy's lottery win—I realized our money and our masters had to be siloed and diversified so a single lawsuit could never touch the family. While we were still recording and touring through Progress Street in 2004, I kept our core capital parked in Treasury ladders while running day-to-day music operations out of Engine Room Records, LLC. The moment we signed off the road after Last Bus Home in late 2004 to recover from burnout, I spent the next eleven years executing that 1997 blueprint—spinning off Stardust Strategic Assets, LLC for the hard equipment and coaches, Artists First Management, LLC for touring liability, and Stardust Properties, LLC and Pacific Rim Properties, LLC for real estate."

"Unbundling Engine Room Records into specialized LLCs between 2004 and 2015 kept our operations clean," Holly continued, "but right now, most of those entities are still registered in Virginia. If a reporter, or a rival executive, or a hostile litigator goes to the Virginia State Corporation Commission website and pays twenty dollars, they can see everything. They can pull the Articles of Organization. They see my name as the Registered Agent. They see our home address."

Holly pulled a marker out of her pocket and drew a large circle on the whiteboard.

"Right now, if someone pulls the thread on the indie band that lives in Blacksburg, that thread leads directly to a $2.4 billion commercial real estate portfolio. It leads to the student housing. It leads to Cassidy's lottery win. We are sitting ducks for a nuisance lawsuit."

Tyler crossed his arms, his biceps straining against his CPI t-shirt. "So, what does Delaware do?"

The Delaware Advantage

1. Absolute Anonymity: Delaware law does not require the names of the LLC members (owners) or managers to be disclosed on the formation documents. The only name on the public registry is the "Registered Agent."

2. The Court of Chancery: Corporate disputes in Delaware do not go to a jury trial where a slick lawyer can play on a jury's emotions. They go to the Court of Chancery—a court consisting solely of specialized corporate judges. Cases are resolved based on strict contract law, not theatrics.

"Delaware makes us ghosts," Holly said, answering Tyler's question. "If we move the entities to Delaware, the state doesn't ask who owns the company. They don't care. The only thing on the public record is the name of the Registered Agent."

"And usually," Holly continued, "billionaires hire third-party law firms to act as their Registered Agents. But third-party firms have paralegals, and paralegals gossip. They leak."

She tapped the Delaware Bar certificate resting on her desk.

"I didn't spend the last eight months studying corporate tax law just for the credential. I took the Bar so I can be the Registered Agent. Every single entity in our portfolio is going to be folded into a Delaware LLC, and I am the only lawyer with the keys."

The Execution

Holly handed out the heavy, black pens.

"We are dissolving the Virginia corporations tonight," she instructed, her voice dropping into its pure, unyielding 'Shark' register. "You are signing the Operating Agreements for the new Delaware entities."

She slid the first stack to Cassidy. "Artists First Management, LLC. This holds the touring contracts and the payroll. It's the shield that takes the hit if someone slips on a cable at a show."

She slid the next stack to Ryan. "Engine Room Records, LLC. This holds the master tapes and the copyrights. The vault."

Evan and Tyler received the real estate stacks. "Stardust Properties, LLC and Pacific Rim Properties, LLC. The cash engines. Completely firewalled from the music."

Finally, she placed a master document in the center of the table.

"And above it all, The O'Connell Family Revocable Trust. The sovereign entity that owns all the LLCs. No one outside this room will ever see this piece of paper."

Notary Protocol Executed

Because Holly obtained her Notary Public commission in 1994, no outside witnesses were required. The family signed the documents in absolute privacy. Holly stamped and sealed the formation of a $2.4 Billion empire without a single outsider knowing it happened.

Ryan signed his name with a fluid, practiced motion. He capped his pen and tossed it onto the table. He looked at his sister, realizing the sheer magnitude of the armor she had just bolted onto them.

"So," Ryan said, a slow, dangerous grin spreading across his face. "We're a multi-billion dollar conglomerate, but on paper, we're just an indie band from Virginia?"

"Exactly," Holly said, gathering the signed documents and walking toward the massive fireproof safe in the corner of the office. "If anyone tries to buy us, sue us, or exploit us, they're going to think they're dealing with five aging musicians."

She spun the dial on the safe, the heavy steel tumblers locking into place with a definitive, echoing CLACK.

"Let them think it. The iceberg is officially submerged."
